title: Wonton, dumpling or fried pot sticker

content.title: About
content.content: Wonton is a traditional Asian dish consisting of thinly rolled dough filled with meat, seafood, vegetables, or a combination, then fried until golden. The “pot sticker” version is often served with soy sauce, vinegar, and chili.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wonton originates from Chinese cuisine, but similar items exist in Japan (gyoza) and Korea (mandu).
The dough is made from simple flour and water without leavening, giving it great elasticity.
Fried pot stickers become crispy on the bottom and tender on top thanks to the steam‑fry technique.
Traditional fillings include soy sauce, ginger, garlic, and green onion for flavor depth.
In China, wontons are often served in broth as soup, while in Japan they are popular as fried appetizers.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Meat, fish or tofu fillings provide complete proteins essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Ingredients such as meat and vegetables contain B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meaty fillings help maintain hemoglobin levels and prevent anemia.

items.title: Low in carbs in the wrapper
items.content: The thin flour wrapper has fewer carbohydrates than thicker dough products, making wonton moderately caloric.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Vegetable additions (cabbage, carrot, mushrooms) supply antioxidants that support the immune system.

items.title: Allergy to seafood or soy sauce
items.content: Fillings may contain shrimp, fish, or soy sauce, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and some seasonings make the dish high in sodium, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Risk of over‑eating
items.content: The crispy texture and savory taste can lead to excessive consumption.

items.title: Trans fats from improper frying
items.content: Using old oil or frying at too high a temperature can create trans fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wontons can be boiled in broth, steamed, or pan‑fried in a small amount of oil until golden. Serve with soy sauce, vinegar, chili oil, or a flavorful broth. They work well as a snack, in salads, or added to soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Raw wontons keep in the refrigerator in an airtight container for 2‑3 days. Frozen raw wontons last up to 3 months. Fried pot stickers are best eaten within 1‑2 days and should be stored in a dry place to retain crispness.
